question: One account traces this place's name to "Saranggong", combining the Malay numeral for "one" with the name of a marsh bird, while another derives it from a phrase meaning "to beat a gong", perhaps to scare off wildlife. In the early nineteenth century Tamil Muslim pioneers settled here, and Indian laborers who worked its lime pits and brick kilns through the 1820s called the area "Soonambu Kambam", or "Village of Lime". From the 1860s to the 1930s its waterways made the area a center for water buffalo, with slaughterhouses and tanneries clustering near a spot called "Kandang Kerbau", or "buffalo enclosure". Starting around 1981, Singapore's Housing and Development Board built this area as one of seven planned estates constructed at the time, alongside Bukit Batok, Jurong East and West, Tampines, Woodlands and Hougang. Its MRT interchange station, served by the Circle and North East lines, sits beneath a mall whose rooftop houses a dog park and Singapore's first library built on a roof. For 10 points, name this district and MRT interchange in Singapore's North-East Region, once home to lime kilns and cattle pens.

A developer called Gold Ridge, incorporated in March 2008 specifically to develop this project, won a competitive government tender for its site that same year. Designed by SAA Architects and built by contractor Low Keng Hua, its roughly 600,000-square-foot interior opened in stages, with a soft launch in November 2010 followed by an official opening the following April. Its rooftop hosts a dog park with separate wet and dry play areas, next to a library that opened on 11 March 2011 as Singapore's first to be built on a rooftop. Anchor tenants have included a Shaw Theatres cinema, a FairPrice Xtra hypermarket, and two rival food courts, Food Junction and Food Republic. It was built directly above the Circle Line platforms of an MRT interchange station in Singapore's North-East Region, with its lowest basement level connecting to an air-conditioned bus interchange. For 10 points, name this shopping mall, home to a rooftop library and dog park, whose seven levels sit above a bus interchange and train station in Singapore's northeast.

Food historian Khir Johari traces this dish to a prewar Singapore kitchen called Rumah Jawa at 51 Sultan Gate, which originally produced satay for stalls across the city. Its gravy traditionally combines tiny dried shrimp called udang geragau with fermented soybean paste called taucheo, thickened with pureed sweet potato. Several towns across the causeway in Malaysia also lay claim to inventing it, with Muar in Johor among the places cited as a possible birthplace. It is typically garnished with beansprouts, slices of fried tofu, a hard-boiled egg and crushed peanuts, plus a wedge of lime and sliced green chilli. Served over flat yellow egg noodles, it is a hawker-stall fixture among Singapore's Malay community, often eaten for breakfast. For 10 points, name this noodle dish served in a thick, sweet-potato-based gravy, a staple of Malay hawker cuisine across Singapore and Malaysia.

Incorporated in May 2004, this halal-certified restaurant has operated around the clock from a shophouse-style building on Kensington Park Road. Its menu includes the "Roti Tsunami", a towering platter piled with chicken curry, mutton curry, dalcha and soft-boiled eggs. Bigger appetites can order its five-litre teh tarik tower, a communal serving of pulled milk tea meant to be shared at the table. Its most famous item is a towering, crispy-yet-fluffy prata that can be topped with chocolate sauce, strawberry, maple syrup or honey, and is meant to be torn apart and shared. Popular with supper crowds and moviegoers, it has become a late-night institution of a private housing estate in Singapore's north-east, prized for its Indian-Muslim food. For 10 points, name this 24-hour restaurant near Chomp Chomp Food Centre, well known for its towering Tissue Prata.
answer: R.K. Eating House [or RK Eating House; prompt on RK or R.K.]

question: The first word of this area's Malay name means a coastal inlet; this district was designated a Chinese district in Stamford Raffles' 1822 town plan for Singapore, though other communities settled there too. Before land reclamation pushed the coastline south in the 1880s using soil dug from Mount Wallich, it was where many newly arrived immigrants disembarked and first set foot in Singapore. Sailors giving thanks for a safe voyage would visit makeshift shrines along its waterfront, a practice that grew into a strip now home to six National Monuments within a few blocks. Those monuments include the Hokkien temple Thian Hock Keng, rebuilt between 1839 and 1842 with donations from junk owners and sailors and dedicated to the sea goddess Mazu. Reclamation eventually left this thoroughfare several blocks from the sea, with newly created land nearby becoming Robinson Road and Shenton Way. For 10 points, name this historic thoroughfare and district in Singapore's Chinatown, once the city's coastal landing point for immigrants arriving by sea.
answer: Telok Ayer [or Telok Ayer Street; accept Telok Ayer Bay or Telok Ayer Basin]

question: Its name comes from a French Antillean Creole word that can mean "party", also used for a genre of dance music from Guadeloupe and Martinique. Restaurateur Lincoln Cheng founded this nightclub in March 1991 after being inspired by trips to Ibiza and other Mediterranean party destinations. It originally occupied three godowns built in 1919 along Jiak Kim Street on the riverfront, restored with new timber trusses while keeping their original walls. Expansions added a room called Velvet Underground in 1994 and a bar called Phuture in 1996, both aimed at young professionals. Credited as the first local club to champion house music over Top 40 hits, it left its Jiak Kim Street home for Clarke Quay in 2016 after twenty-five years there. For 10 points, name this pioneering nightclub, originally located along the river.

This event's second edition was cancelled in 2002 following the Bali bombings, and its 2003 edition briefly relocated to the Marina Bay waterfront. Its tenth-anniversary edition in December 2010 drew a record 28,000 partygoers, prompting organizers to expand to a two-day format from 2012 onward. Headliners over the years have included Tiesto, Armin van Buuren, David Guetta and Martin Garrix, performing across multiple stages spanning genres like trance, house and techno. Attendance peaked around 50,000 in 2014, and the Singapore Tourism Board has honoured it as Best Leisure Event Experience on three occasions between 2005 and 2020. Held annually on Sentosa's Siloso Beach, it was called off in 2020 and 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic before returning in December 2022. For 10 points, name this annual dusk-to-dawn electronic dance festival on Sentosa's Siloso Beach, established by a well-known Singapore nightclub.

Founded in 2012 by Indra Kantono and Guoyi Gan, this bar first operated on Amoy Street before relocating to the lobby of the Amara Hotel in Tanjong Pagar in 2018. It temporarily shut in March 2020 and reopened that September, and in 2023 it won the Best International Hotel Bar award at Tales of the Cocktail. It became the first Singapore venue to be named Asia's number one on the Asia's 50 Best Bars list, in 2020, before settling at third place from 2021 to 2023. Each year the bar releases a lengthy, thematically organized cocktail menu it calls a "menuzine", including a 68-page edition titled "Embrace". Its bartenders serve modern riffs on classics, such as a Paloma made with house-made guava-and-grapefruit soda and an interactive peeled grapefruit wedge. For 10 points, name this award-winning cocktail bar in Tanjong Pagar's Amara Hotel, co-founded by Indra Kantono and Guoyi Gan.
